meta.question: Is the harbor dispute worth a long-form video, and what do we need to get right?

bottom.bluf: A fictional sample. Two port authorities are fighting over harbor rights granted by an 1888 treaty [@ostrova-harbor, p. 4]. The fight is legal, but it now touches shipping insurance and a spring naval exercise.
bottom.takeaways:
The treaty supports both readings; the dispute turns on one clause and its translation. | High
Insurance costs, not the courts, are what shipping firms are reacting to. | Moderate
The spring exercise could turn a legal story into a security story. | Low
bottom.dimensions:
Complexity | High | A 138-year-old treaty, three courts, two languages
Contention | High | Both sides have serious lawyers and serious historians
Source base | Moderate | Rich on the law, thin on the shipping data
Pace of change | Moderate | A ruling is due in the first quarter
Sensitivity | Low | Few personal stakes; little risk of harm

considerations.items:
Accuracy | The treaty exists in two official languages. Quote the clause in both, or say which you used.
Sensitivity | Port workers on both sides have been laid off. Avoid making either town the villain.
Legal | No defamation risk found, but the litigation is live. Do not predict the ruling as fact.
Audience | Viewers will assume this is about oil. It is not, and saying so early is a hook.
Timing | The ruling is expected in the first quarter. A piece before it needs a clear "what happens next."
considerations.misconceptions:
The strait is closed to shipping | Traffic is down about a fifth, not stopped [@reyes-tugboats]
The navy is involved | Not yet. The exercise was planned before the dispute.
The treaty is a dead letter | It was cited in rulings as recently as 2011 [@kell-strait, p. 212].

debates.intro: Historians and lawyers split on the treaty. The split is honest, not partisan.
debates.items:
? Does the treaty cover the outer anchorage?
+ Expansive reading: the Meridian report and the northern authority. The 1888 maps include it.
+ Narrow reading: the southern authority and most historians. The text says "harbor," and the anchorage was not used until 1903.
= The text favors the narrow reading; the maps favor the expansive one. The courts have not settled which wins.
? Is traffic falling because of the dispute?
+ Yes: port officials quoted in the press.
+ Partly: insurers point to a wider slump in regional trade.
= Partly. The dispute explains some of the drop, not all.
debates.gaps:
How much fee revenue is at stake? | The authorities' audited accounts, which are not public
Will the navy change the exercise? | A statement from the defense ministry

report.body:
# Background

The harbor at Valdera has been shared since 1888.^[All names in this sample are invented.] The treaty that set the terms is short and, in places, vague [@kell-strait, pp. 40-44].

>> 1888: the treaty is signed after a decade of tariff disputes.
For most of the twentieth century the arrangement held. Each port collected fees on its own side of the channel and shared dredging costs.

# What the research shows

## The legal question

The dispute turns on whether "the waters of the harbor" includes the outer anchorage [@ostrova-harbor, p. 11]. If it does, one authority has been collecting fees it is not owed.

!> The fight is over a clause, a translation, and about forty million a year in fees.

[[traffic]]

## The economic effect

Shipping firms have rerouted some traffic, mostly on the advice of insurers [@reyes-tugboats]. Port employment has fallen on both sides.

# Angles and story leads

{Angle 1} The translation: one word, two meanings, forty million a year.
{Angle 2} The insurers: the quiet players moving ships.
{Watch} The first-quarter ruling, and the spring exercise.
